3. A tree with two nodes claiming the same order position or the same block twice in one list fails.
4. Round-trip of every fixture is lossless, including empty books, empty regions and a book whose
   structure is only a title.
5. ID generation never yields `0`, never collides across two books that are validated together, and
   is unaffected by a placement change.
6. Title normalization strips `1.`, `1.1`, `1.1.1` and `IV.` prefixes and leaves `2026 – Year of X`
   and `3D Printing` unchanged (the latter is a test case, not an assumption).
7. `part` is representable on a chapter or link and rejected on a subchapter or block.
8. The model package imports neither `internal/cli`, nor `internal/store`, nor any IO package.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-3"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- ID representation: integer, string, or a typed value with a namespace prefix. Decide the one shape
  that survives global uniqueness and JSON.
- Whether node and block IDs share one counter/namespace with globally unique values, or use disjoint
  prefixes. `PLAN.md` requires global uniqueness; the encoding is open.
- Where the next-ID allocator lives: the model cannot allocate without the registry (S11) or the
  store (S04). Decide the interface and the owner.
- How `link` entries are represented (target book/node/block, title for display) and whether a link
  can be a block instead of a manifest entry.
- Manifest JSON: one document versus split documents (structure, settings, regions). Affects
  container members in S04 and lock granularity in S06.
- Whether `part` uniqueness is validated in the model (part-wise output needs unique parts) or only
  at render time in S09.
- Region collection shape: one collection type with a target discriminator, or a node-attached
  collection field. `PLAN.md` says regions are blocks in an ordered collection with a target.
- `index.depth`, `toc` and `output` enum values: define them here so S09 can consume them.


<a id="risks-and-constraints-3"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- The model is the contract every other scope compiles against. Changes after S04 are expensive;
  spend the design budget on the ID representation, the placement lists and the manifest split.
- `PLAN.md` forbids structural bodies. Do not add a compatibility field for "chapter body"; the hard
  cut means no legacy shape has to be representable.
- Block ID `0` is a sentinel, never data. Do not encode it as "unset" in a way that can round-trip
  into storage.
- Keep the model free of file paths. A book's output path belongs to the store and the registry.


<a id="s04-central-store-and-containers"></a>

## S04 — Central Store and Containers ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S04a (container codec, delivered) -> S04b (store
layout, book identity, hash pairs, delivered) -> S04c (registry, diff, export, delivered).
Phase: 3. Depends on: S02 (paths), S03 (model). Blocks: S05, S06, S07, S08, S09, S11.
PLAN refs: §3.2 (central store), §3.7 (store layout, extracted bodies, rollback location), §6
(deterministic containers, drift detection), §2.1 (current container shape), §2.5 (defect to avoid).


<a id="goal-4"></a>

### Goal

Make the store the single durable home of all working data — one configurable root, a deterministic
book container per book, a registry, terms, rollback storage and layout sources — with byte-identical
round-trips, per-member hashes and drift detection, and without any book semantics.


<a id="in-scope-4"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One store root (default `_CLABOK`, configurable in S02); the docs path carries rendered output only, no `_source` folders | §3.2 |
| 2 | Fixed layout below the root: `<bookId>/`, `<bookId>/blocks/` (extracted bodies, above S05), `<bookId>/layouts/`, `rollback/<bookId>/`, the registry, `terms.txt` | §3.7 |
| 3 | Book identity is decoupled from the output path: the book ID names the store folder; the output path is an attribute, not the identity | §3.2 |
| 4 | Container: deterministic encoding with fixed member order, fixed timestamp and a per-member SHA-256; re-saving an unchanged book is byte-identical | §6 |
| 5 | Reader/writer API: read all members, read one member, write a member set, verify checksums, reject a tampered or truncated container with a stable error | §6 |
| 6 | Input/output hash pairs per book, stored where `sync --check` and `book status` can compare them without re-rendering | §6 |
| 7 | `diff` between two container states (member-level added/changed/removed) and `export` of container members to a directory | §5, §3.13 |
| 8 | Registry persistence primitives (file read/write, atomic replace, version field); registry semantics and policy belong to S11 | §3.2, §3.7 |
| 9 | `terms.txt` and layout sources live in the store; their content semantics belong to S12 and S13 | §3.2, §3.14 |
| 10 | Atomic file writes for every store mutation (temp sibling + rename), with the same guarantees on Windows and Unix | §6 |
| 11 | No absolute paths inside the container; no machine-specific metadata; no timestamps that break determinism | §6 |
| 12 | `.gitignore` already excludes `_CLABOK/` and `.temp/`; the store must not require additional ignore rules | §3.2, §3.3 |


<a id="out-of-scope-5"></a>

### Out of scope

- Open/close state machine, extraction lifecycle and rollback tier policy: S05.
- Locking and multi-process coordination: S06.
- Registry entries, library policy and defaults: S11.
- Rendering, output hashing from a render pass and `sync` behaviour: S09 (it consumes the hash API).
- Temp input handling and `flush`: S08.
- Terms content and grammar: S13. Layout block content: S12.
- Any read of legacy `Assets/Docs` containers: excluded by the hard cut.


<a id="deliverables-4"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/store`: container codec, member hashing, atomic writer, book hash pairs, store layout
  resolution from the S02 config.
- `internal/store`: `diff` and `export` primitives.
- Registry file codec with a version field and atomic replace (semantics delegated to S11).
- Error codes for: container corrupt, checksum mismatch, member missing, store not found, store not
  writable, absolute path in container, write conflict.
- Fixture containers (minimal, nested, large, corrupted, truncated) under `testdata/`.
- Benchmark for container write/read to catch accidental quadratic behaviour.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-4"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. Create a book container, read it back, write it unchanged: the bytes are identical (golden file
   and SHA-256 comparison).
2. Reordering the in-memory member map does not change the output; a test permutes insertion order.
3. A corrupted member, a truncated file and a wrong checksum each fail with a distinct stable code
   and never return partial data as success.
4. A container written on Windows reads identically on Linux in CI (fixture is committed).
5. `diff` reports added, changed and removed members between two states.
6. `export` writes exactly the members and paths of the container.
7. A failed write leaves the previous container intact (simulated failure between temp write and
   rename).
8. The store root resolves from the S02 config; two books in one store do not share any mutable file.
9. No package reads the store root from the working directory or from the environment.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-4"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- Container encoding: standard `archive/zip` with normalized headers versus a custom framed format.
  `PLAN.md` fixes determinism, not the encoding. Check that the chosen encoding can pin the member
  timestamp and the compression level.
- Member layout: one manifest member plus `blocks/<id>.md`, or a per-node manifest split. It follows
  the manifest decision from S03.
- Checksum member: a separate checksum index member, or a checksum per member entry in the archive
  comment. Decide the tamper evidence.
- Hash pair definition: what exactly is hashed for "input" and "output" (manifest bytes, body bytes,
  rendered bytes) and where the pair is stored (book folder vs registry).
- Registry file format and versioning; how a registry entry records the output path, kind, and the
  library's own policy fields.
- How `bookId` is derived (slug, assigned number, hash) and whether it is user-visible.
- Whether `export` is a first-delivery command or a later convenience (it is not required by any
  `PLAN.md` statement; keep it small).
- Compression level and its effect on determinism and size.


<a id="risks-and-constraints-4"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- The reference implementation's `body list --json` defect (§2.5) comes from storing the parent
  object where a depth number is expected. Any "list" API in the store must expose a hashable or
  serializable shape; add a golden JSON test for every list command.
- Determinism is easy to lose through map iteration and `time.Now()`. Pin both in the codec and test
  them.
- Windows rename semantics differ from Unix; the atomic writer needs its own test on both platforms.
- The store is a working area, not a backup. Rollback packages are the safety net (S05), not the
  store's job.


<a id="s05-open-close-lifecycle-and-rollback-tiers"></a>

## S05 — Open/Close Lifecycle and Rollback Tiers ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S05a (open/close mechanics, open state,
extraction, repack, recovery, delivered) and S05b (rollback tiers, crash reporting, delivered).
Phase: 3. Depends on: S04 (container, store layout), S06 (coordinator interface). Blocks: S07, S08,
S11, S14.
PLAN refs: §3.5 (complete lifecycle), §3.7 (open state, extracted bodies, rollback, immovability),
§6 (open/close safety, rollback for every write).


<a id="goal-5"></a>

### Goal

Define and enforce the book lifecycle: a closed book is a packed container, an open book is extracted
authoritative body files, every writer creates an undo package, closing repacks deterministically,
and a crash is reported instead of repaired.


<a id="in-scope-5"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `open <book>` extracts all body data; every body read and write requires an open book; a closed book is not readable | §3.5 |
| 2 | Extracted body files are authoritative while open; the container is not consulted until close | §3.5 |
| 3 | `close <book>` repacks deterministically; closing an unchanged book creates no book-level rollback point | §3.5 |
| 4 | Idempotence: `open` on an open book and `close` on a closed book succeed without side effects; errors are reserved for real errors | §3.5 |
| 5 | Multiple books may be open; open and close take an explicit book and never touch another open book; a second `open` creates no second extracted state | §3.5 |
| 6 | Open state is tracked, not inferred: a state file keyed by book ID records output path, pid or session, and timestamp | §3.7 |
| 7 | Every mutating command creates an undo-capable rollback package; undo packages are capped (default 10, S02) and deleted when the book closes | §3.5, §3.7 |
| 8 | Closing creates a book-level rollback point only if the book changed; at most 3 are kept, oldest evicted (limits from S02) | §3.5 |
| 9 | Crash state: when extracted changes are newer than the container, report the state and deliver the readable content directly; no separate recover or repair command | §3.5 |
| 10 | `check` and `verify` report an open book as a non-blocking `open-book` finding that does not change the exit code; `book status` shows the open state; `sync --check` stays a drift check | §3.5 |
| 11 | An open book cannot be moved, renamed or unregistered | §3.7 |
| 12 | An interrupted open or close is detectable and never corrupts the container | §6 |
| 13 | Close coordinates with in-flight block edits: it waits for or rejects them and never repacks a body being written | §3.12 (coordination owned by S06) |
| 14 | The lifecycle works under both coordination backends with identical semantics | §3.5, §3.12 |


<a id="out-of-scope-6"></a>

### Out of scope

- Lock primitives, backends and lock ordering: S06.
- Container codec, checksums and atomic writes: S04.
- Which commands mutate and therefore need an undo package: the owning scopes (S07, S08, S12) call
  the rollback API provided here.
- Book settings and structure commands: S07.
- Renderer and `sync --write`/`--prune`: S09.
- Registry entry updates on move/rename: S11 (this scope only enforces the refusal).


<a id="deliverables-5"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/store` lifecycle (or a dedicated lifecycle package): open, close, state file, extraction,
  repack, change detection.
- `open.json` state codec with atomic replace and a recovery view for a stale entry.
- Rollback API: create undo package, list, restore, evict, delete-on-close, book-level point with cap.
- `book` command subgroup for `open`, `close`, `status` (settings stay in S07).
- `open-book` finding integration point used by `check`/`verify`.
- Tests: crash simulation (process killed between extract and close), double open, close without
  open, close without changes, cap enforcement, eviction order, immovability refusals.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-5"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. `open` twice in two processes results in one extracted state and one state entry; the second call
   is a no-op.
2. A body read on a closed book fails with a stable `book.not-open` code; no fallback to the
   container.
3. `close` after a body edit repacks the change; `sync --check` equivalents see the new state.
4. `close` on an unchanged book writes no book-level rollback point; the container is byte-identical.
5. Undo packages stop at the configured limit and are removed by `close`; book rollback points stop
   at three and evict the oldest.
6. Killing the process after an extraction but before a close reports the crash state on the next
   command and delivers the extracted content read-only through the normal pipeline.
7. A corrupt or half-written state file is detected and reported; the container is still readable.
8. Moving, renaming or unregistering an open book is refused with a stable code.
9. `check` reports `open-book` without changing the exit code; `book status` shows the open state.
10. An interrupted close (kill between repack and state cleanup) leaves a readable container and a
    state that the next command can reconcile without a repair command.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-5"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- `open.json` shape and atomicity; whether the state file lives per store or per book folder.
- Session identity: pid plus start time, a session token, or both. How a dead pid is recognized on
  Windows and Unix, and whether takeover is automatic or requires an explicit `open` after a report.
- What "changed" means for the book-level rollback point (manifest hash, body hash, or the S04 hash
  pair).
- Undo package content and naming; whether a package is a full snapshot or a delta, and how restore
  interacts with an open book.
- Whether close is refused while another process holds a block lock, or waits (S06 provides the
  primitive; the policy is decided here).
- Does `close` prune an empty undo directory, and does `open` delete a stale extracted folder from a
  previous crash or keep it for inspection?
- Where the readable-content-delivery path surfaces: `book status`, `check`, or both.
- Whether `open` allocates the book's output path in the registry (coordination with S11).


<a id="risks-and-constraints-5"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- Crash handling is the hardest part. Model it with a test that can kill the process at defined
  points instead of reasoning about it.
- The lifecycle must not become a hidden second storage mode. `PLAN.md` explicitly replaces the
  storage-mode setting with open/close; there is no `--storage` flag.
- Rollback is the safety net for every write. A missing package on an unexpected error path is a
  defect, not a nicety; test the error path, not only the success path.


<a id="s06-concurrency-and-coordination"></a>

## S06 — Concurrency and Coordination ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S06a (coordinator interface, file backend,
delivered) and S06b (daemon, mode selection, version handshake, conformance suite, delivered).
Phase: 3. Depends on: S04 (store, atomic writes). Blocks: S05, S07, S08, S12, S14.
PLAN refs: §3.12 (complete), §3.5 (close coordination), §3.7 (stale and concurrent changes),
§6 (identical backend semantics, per-block concurrency, stable lock order).


<a id="goal-6"></a>

### Goal

Provide one coordinator contract with two interchangeable backends — file locks and an in-memory
`pecia serve` daemon — so that concurrent authoring in two processes is safe, per-block edits run in
parallel, structural changes serialize per node, and no backend changes book data.


<a id="in-scope-6"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One coordinator interface consumed by book logic; the core never depends on a backend | §3.12 |
| 2 | `file` backend (default): lock files, atomic writes, stale detection | §3.12 |
| 3 | `daemon` backend: in-memory mutexes in one `pecia serve` process, same binary, a mode not a second product | §3.12 |
| 4 | Identical semantics for both: one writer per locked resource, consistent reader snapshots, no lost writes, stale-session detection | §3.12, §6 |
| 5 | Granularity: body edits lock one block ID; manifest changes lock the affected structural node or the book's structure lock (add, remove, rename, move, reparent, reorder) | §3.12 |
| 6 | Lock ordering: multi-lock operations acquire book -> node -> block with timeouts, so crossing moves cannot deadlock | §3.12 |
| 7 | Reads use an atomic snapshot and need no write lock; a reader never sees a half-written block | §3.12 |
| 8 | Close coordination: a close waits for or rejects in-flight block edits and never repacks a body being written | §3.12 |
| 9 | Mode selection from S02 (`concurrency.mode`), CLI flags override; switching the mode while a book is open is rejected | §3.12 |
| 10 | Daemon transport is local only: one AF_UNIX socket on every platform (owner decision 2026-11-05); no TCP listener | §3.12 |
| 11 | The CLI expects a running daemon in `daemon` mode and fails with a clear error when it is absent; it never auto-starts one | §3.12 |
| 12 | CLI and daemon must run the same version; a mismatch is a clear error | §3.12 |
| 13 | The backend never changes book data, IDs, rendering or output | §3.12 |
| 14 | A shared conformance suite runs the same semantics test against both backends | §6 |


<a id="out-of-scope-7"></a>

### Out of scope

- Open/close state machine and lifecycle policy: S05 (it consumes the coordinator).
- Which command acquires which lock: declared by S07, S08 and S12; this scope provides the primitive
  and the ordering helper.
- Remote or network coordination: explicitly excluded by `PLAN.md`.
- Daemon management UI or service installation; `serve` is a process mode, nothing more.
- TUI concurrency behaviour: S14.


<a id="deliverables-6"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/coordinator`: interface, resource identity (book, node, block), lock ordering helper,
  timeout and stale-session errors, reader snapshot contract.
- `internal/coordinator/file`: lock files, stale detection, atomic write integration.
- `internal/coordinator/daemon`: client plus server (`pecia serve`) and the local transport
  (`_windows.go`, `_unix.go` with build tags).
- Conformance test suite parameterized by backend.
- Multi-process integration tests using tiny helper binaries or re-exec of the test binary.
- Version handshake between CLI and daemon.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-6"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. Two processes edit two different blocks of the same structural node concurrently; both writes land.
2. Two processes write the same block; one wins, the other fails with a stable conflict or stale
   code, and no write is lost or merged.
3. Two crossing moves (A into B's subtree while B moves into A's) cannot deadlock: the test terminates
   within the configured timeout and one operation is rejected.
4. A reader during a concurrent write never observes a partial body (test reads in a tight loop while
   a writer rewrites a large body).
5. A stale lock from a dead process is reclaimed after the configured timeout, under both backends.
6. Close during an in-flight body write either waits and repacks the final state or rejects the close;
   it never repacks a partial body.
7. Switching `concurrency.mode` while a book is open is refused.
8. In `daemon` mode without a running server, a mutating command fails with a clear error and does
   not auto-start anything.
9. A CLI/daemon version mismatch is refused with the two versions in the message.
10. The conformance suite is green against both backends, including on Windows.
11. `go test -race` is clean for the whole repository.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-6"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- Lock file content: owner identity, session token, lease deadline, and the staleness criterion
  (heartbeat versus timeout versus pid liveness).
- Timeout defaults and whether they are configurable (S02 currently lists only the mode and the
  socket path; adding a timeout is an owner decision if it should be user-visible).
- Named pipe name and Unix socket path defaults, and their derivation from the project path.
- Daemon lifecycle: start, readiness, idle timeout, shutdown, and what happens to open books when the
  daemon stops (the state file is the truth; decide the report).
- Whether the daemon is stateless apart from mutexes and book snapshots, or caches books.
- Snapshot semantics for reads: whole manifest, per file, or per book folder.
- How the coordinator interface exposes a multi-lock operation (a callback that receives all locks,
  or explicit acquire/release with ordering enforced by the helper).
- Whether lock files live in the store or the temp area (`PLAN.md` does not fix it; they are transient
  and must not be committed, which argues for the temp area).


<a id="risks-and-constraints-6"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- File locking on Windows and Unix differs. Test on both; do not assume POSIX semantics.
- A daemon that caches state becomes a second source of truth. Keep the book state in the store and
  limit the daemon to coordination.
- Stale detection is the failure mode that produces lost writes. Test with a real killed process, not
  a simulated flag.
- Backend parity is an invariant. Any behaviour that only one backend can produce is a bug.


<a id="s07-structure-and-book-settings-commands"></a>

## S07 — Structure and Book Settings Commands ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S07a (add, rename, move, remove, book settings,
delivered) and S07b (declarative `apply` plans, delivered).
Phase: 4. Depends on: S03 (model), S04 (store), S05 (open state), S06 (locks). Blocks: S08, S09, S11,
S14.
PLAN refs: §3.7 (uniform commands, placement, move arguments, reparenting, settings live with the
book, no pin), §3 (4, 9, 10), §3.14 (no pin), §6 (rollback for every write).


<a id="goal-7"></a>

### Goal

Deliver the complete structure-authoring surface: uniform `add`, `rename`, `move`, `remove` over
nodes and blocks, explicit placement, reparenting across levels, and the book-settings commands that
replace direct manifest editing — all through locks, dry-run and rollback.


<a id="in-scope-7"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `add`, `rename`, `move`, `remove` operate on structure nodes and blocks; the node type follows the target parent (book -> chapter, chapter -> subchapter, subchapter -> block); no per-type commands | §3.7 |
| 2 | Placement is list order: a node or region holds an ordered block-ID list; blocks carry no placement data; a move edits two lists and never touches a body | §3.7 |
| 3 | Chapters and subchapters have an order among their siblings; reordering and reparenting of chapter and subchapter nodes stay possible | §3 (4), §3.7 |
| 4 | Move arguments: `--child-of <node>` appends, `--index N` places explicitly, `--before/--after <block-id>` places relatively | §3.7 |
| 5 | Reparenting keeps the node ID and its block list; its children move with it; a move that would create a fourth structural level is rejected | §3.7 |
| 6 | Moving a block assigns its placement and keeps its body byte-identical and its ID unchanged | §3 (4) |
| 7 | Book settings commands for `numbering`, `toc`, `index.depth` and `output`: stored in the book manifest, changed only through commands; the library holds defaults and policy, never per-book values | §3.7 |
| 8 | `pin` is removed; the generated index follows the structure order | §3.7 |
| 9 | Declarative batch plans (`apply`): a validated, atomic plan covering structure and content, with one rollback point, delegating to the same services as the individual commands | §3.13 (`internal/apply`) |
| 10 | Every mutating command: `--dry-run` receipt, rollback package (S05), lock per S06, requires an open book (S05), rejects stale state | §3.12, §6 |
| 11 | Stable error codes for: unknown target, wrong parent type, level limit, duplicate title within a parent, invalid index, dangling block ID, stale state, closed book | §3.7 |
| 12 | JSON responses include the resulting order (affected lists) so tooling does not have to re-read the book | §3.10 |


<a id="out-of-scope-8"></a>

### Out of scope

- Body text and body writes: S08.
- Rendering, heading emission, index generation, mode switches: S09.
- Numbering semantics, anchor derivation, reference rewriting: S10.
- Library-level defaults and their application across books: S11.
- ID allocation internals: S03 (model) plus the store/registry owner; this scope calls the allocator.
- Applying a plan's prose bodies: the content part of `apply` calls S08's body service.


<a id="deliverables-7"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/structure`: add, rename, move, remove, reorder, reparent, invariants, dry-run receipts.
- `internal/cli` command group for the four commands and for the settings commands under `book`.
- `internal/apply`: plan schema, validation, atomic execution, one rollback point.
- Tests: a matrix per command and node type; move argument combinations; level-limit rejections;
  body-identity assertion after a block move; dry-run leaves the book byte-identical; rollback after
  a failed plan.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-7"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. `add` creates the type dictated by the parent: a chapter under the book, a subchapter under a
   chapter, a block under a subchapter; an attempt to add a chapter under a subchapter is refused.
2. Moving a chapter with children moves the whole subtree; IDs and block lists are unchanged.
3. A move that would create a fourth structural level fails with a stable code and changes nothing.
4. `--child-of`, `--index`, `--before` and `--after` each place the unit exactly; a combination that
   is contradictory is rejected before writing.
5. Moving a block between two nodes leaves both bodies byte-identical (hash comparison).
6. `--dry-run` produces a receipt and leaves the container and the extracted bodies byte-identical.
7. A failing `apply` plan leaves no partial change: one rollback point, the book is as before.
8. `book set numbering|toc|index.depth|output` round-trips through the manifest; an invalid enum value
   is refused; the command works only on an open book.
9. `pin` is absent from the command surface and from the manifest schema.
10. A closed book rejects every structure command with `book.not-open`.
11. Two processes adding to the same chapter serialize; the final order is one of the two valid
    orders, never a lost entry.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-7"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- `remove` on a node with children: cascade, reject, or require an explicit `--recursive`. `PLAN.md`
  does not decide it; pick one and state the rationale.
- Whether `add` can create a node together with its first blocks, or creates the node only.
- Exact command grammar: positional arguments versus flags for the target and the title, and how a
  block target is distinguished from a node target.
- How `--before/--after` behave when the reference block is in another node (reject, or move into the
  referenced block's node).
- Whether a title must be unique within its parent (the model may allow duplicates; the renderer
  anchors must stay unique, which S10 solves; decide whether uniqueness is a hard rule).
- `apply` plan schema and whether it is versioned like the config.
- Whether settings commands accept the value as a positional or a flag, and how `index.depth` is
  bounded.
- Receipt shape for a move: the two affected lists, or the whole affected subtree.


<a id="risks-and-constraints-7"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- The uniform command surface is a product statement. Do not add `add-chapter`, `move-block` or other
  per-type aliases.
- Structure changes are the highest-risk mutations. Every one needs a rollback package and a dry-run
  receipt, including the successful path.
- Do not let `apply` become a second implementation of structure logic; it must call the same
  services.


<a id="s08-body-authoring-prose-discipline-and-temp"></a>

## S08 — Body Authoring, Prose Discipline and Temp ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S08a (body commands, prose discipline, block
parallelism, delivered) and S08b (temp area, flush, find, delivered).
Phase: 4. Depends on: S03 (model), S04 (store), S05 (open state, rollback), S06 (locks).
Blocks: S09, S13, S14.
PLAN refs: §3 statements 3, 5, 6; §3.3 (temp area), §3.7 (body writes), §2.5 (defect to avoid),
§3.14 (terms and grammar gate call site).


<a id="goal-8"></a>

### Goal

Deliver prose authoring against the block pool: write, read, replace and find text in blocks with the
block-ID rule, enforce that bodies contain no structural headings (`#`, `##`, `###`) while `####` and
deeper is text, and keep transient authoring inputs in the project `.temp` area.


<a id="in-scope-8"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bodies belong to blocks only; there is no structural body and no chapter or subchapter text | §3 (3) |
| 2 | Body commands: read (block, line range), `set`, `append`, `prepend`, `replace` (single and batch), `list` | §5, §3.13 (`internal/body`) |
| 3 | Block-ID rule: a body-writing command always takes a block ID; `0` appends a new block to the target chapter or subchapter; a valid ID overwrites that block's body; an invalid ID is rejected; the target is required for `0` and an existing block is never moved | §3.7 |
| 4 | Prose discipline: a body must not contain `#`, `##` or `###`; `####` and deeper are text, not a body unit and not a structural level | §3 (5, 6) |
| 5 | The heading rule is checkable at write time and as part of read-only acceptance; code fences are not prose headings (decide the exact rule) | §3 (6) |
| 6 | Prose headings never become structural: ToC generation and lint treat them as text (the rule is defined here, the implementation lands in S09) | §3 (6) |
| 7 | Temp area: `<tempRoot>/<bookId>/` with `tempRoot` from S02 (default `.temp/` at the project root); transient authoring inputs only; durable data stays in the store | §3.3 |
| 8 | `flush` lists stale temp inputs; deletion happens only after explicit confirmation, `--all` is the explicit project-wide sweep; it never touches the store | §3.3, §3.13 |
| 9 | `find` over bodies and manifests: fields (body, title, note, prose), context lines, count versus occurrences, case sensitivity, whole-word, files-only | §3.13 (`internal/search`) |
| 10 | UTF-8 validation, BOM refusal, and end-of-line normalization to the repository convention (`end_of_line = lf`) before a body is stored | §3.10 (determinism), `.editorconfig` |
| 11 | Every write: grammar gate hook (S13), rollback package (S05), block lock (S06), open-book requirement (S05), dry-run | §3.14, §6 |
| 12 | `body list` emits a JSON shape that is serializable for nested books: depth is a number and no domain object leaks into the response | §2.5 |


<a id="out-of-scope-9"></a>

### Out of scope

- Structure commands (add/move/remove of nodes) and settings: S07.
- Rendering bodies, output modes and heading emission: S09.
- Numbering and anchors: S10.
- Grammar engine, LanguageTool client and terms flow: S13 (this scope owns the call site and the
  policy switch, not the checker).
- Notes, status and other editorial regions: S12.
- Temp cleanup policy beyond `flush`; no size limit or scheduled cleanup in `PLAN.md`.


<a id="deliverables-8"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/body`: read, write, replace, block-ID resolution, heading rule, encoding normalization.
- `internal/temp`: temp root resolution, per-book folder, `flush` listing and confirmed deletion.
- `internal/search`: `find` over bodies and manifest fields.
- `internal/cli` command group `body` and the `find` command.
- Tests: block-ID matrix, heading matrix, batch replace atomicity, find filters, flush dry-run and
  confirmation, encoding rejection, nested `body list` JSON golden.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-8"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. `0` appends a new block to the named chapter or subchapter; the new block is returned with its ID
   and appears in the node's ordered list.
2. A valid block ID overwrites exactly that body; the block's placement and the order of siblings are
   unchanged.
3. An invalid block ID, a missing target for `0`, and a target that is not a chapter or subchapter
   each fail with a distinct stable code.
4. A body containing `#`, `##` or `###` is refused with a stable code; a body containing `####` or
   deeper is accepted and stored verbatim.
5. A batch `replace` with an expected occurrence count either applies all pairs or none; the rollback
   package restores the previous bodies.
6. `body list` on a nested book emits valid JSON with numeric depth; a golden test covers the shape
   (the §2.5 defect class).
7. `flush` without confirmation deletes nothing; with confirmation it removes only files under the
   temp root of the current store/config scope.
8. `find` reports counts and occurrences separately; `--context`, `--word`, `--case-sensitive` and
   `--files` behave as documented.
9. A CRLF body is stored with LF endings; a BOM is rejected with a stable code.
10. Every body write creates a rollback package and requires an open book; a closed book rejects the
    write.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-8"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- Forbidden headings: hard error, or error with an explicit override; and where the check runs
  (write, `check`, render, or all three).
- Heading detection inside fenced code blocks and inside HTML comments: how much Markdown parsing is
  acceptable without a full parser dependency.
- Whether a body may start with a `####` heading (the legacy `ahadv` pattern). `PLAN.md` classifies
  it as text; decide whether it is allowed in new prose or only documented as a legacy exception.
- `body replace` semantics: literal versus regex, replacement order and conflict handling when two
  pairs match the same region, and the meaning of `--expect N`.
- Empty bodies: allowed, refused, or normalized away.
- Body size limits (if any), and whether a huge body is split by the author or by a command.
- Temp layout: per book only, or also per command run; what `flush` considers stale (age, session,
  or "not referenced by an open book").
- `find` over manifest fields requires no open book? Decide whether it works on a closed book by
  reading the container (it does not write, and S05 forbids body reads on a closed book; reads of
  bodies must respect that rule).


<a id="risks-and-constraints-8"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- The heading rule is the boundary between prose and structure. If it is implemented as a rewrite
  (the reference implementation shifts headings), the model breaks. It must be a validation, never a
  transformation.
- `body list --json` is the reference defect named in `PLAN.md` §2.5. Test the nested case explicitly.
- Temp inputs must never become durable data by accident. `flush` deletes; the store does not.
- Do not introduce a Markdown parser dependency for the heading rule without an owner decision.


<a id="s09-rendering-and-output-modes"></a>

## S09 — Rendering and Output Modes ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S09a (render modes, index, sync, check) and S09b (ASCII UI catalog, anchor rendering). The index-prose field arrives with S12.
Phase: 5. Depends on: S04 (store), S07 (structure, settings), S08 (bodies). Blocks: S10, S11, S12, S14.
PLAN refs: §3.4 (modes), §3.7 (rendering between blocks, mode switches, heading mapping, navigation,
no pin), §3 (7), §3.14 (index prose rendering), §6 (deterministic output, drift detection, `check`).


<a id="goal-9"></a>

### Goal

Turn a book into deterministic Markdown in one of three modes, with generated structural headings,
a generated index in the README, per-file navigation and pruning of files a mode no longer produces.


<a id="in-scope-9"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `README.md` is always rendered and always carries the document index | §3 (7), §3.4 |
| 2 | Monolith is the default: one rendered `README.md` with the index followed by the full book text | §3.4 |
| 3 | Chapter-wise: one generated file per chapter plus a generated index in the README | §3.4 |
| 4 | Part-wise (opt-in, reversible): one generated file per part, using the existing `part` grouping; README lists chapters grouped by part and links into the part files; a book without parts cannot use it; every chapter carries a `part` value in that mode | §3.4 |
| 5 | Part file names derive deterministically from the part value; generated files are never hand-renamed; part values are unique within a book | §3.4 |
| 6 | Region collections present in the model render at their target position: the book footer slot, directly beneath a node or block for notes, and on the entry for index prose. The placement contract lives here; authoring, status vocabulary and badge detection live in S12 | §3.14 |
| 7 | Heading mapping per mode: monolith README `#`/`##`/`###`; part file `#`/`##`/`###`; chapter file `#`/`##` | §3.7 |
| 8 | Structural headings are generated from the manifest and never authored; a prose `####` or deeper is rendered verbatim as body text and never enters the ToC or the structural hierarchy | §3 (6), §3.7 |
| 9 | Index generation: entries in structure order, `part` as an index-only bold grouping line (no heading, no numbering effect), optional index prose per entry, no pin | §3 (10), §3.14, §3.7 |
| 10 | Rendering between blocks: one blank line, no separator markers | §3.7 |
| 11 | Split files keep per-file navigation and ToC: previous/index/next at the top and bottom with `---` separators, previous/next omitted at boundaries, `**Contents**` before the H1 when `toc` is enabled. The README carries the Document Index link (library) or the Library link plus the first-document link in split modes | §3.7, §3.14 |
| 12 | Mode switching is reversible; `sync --prune` removes generated files a mode no longer produces | §3.7, §3.4 |
| 13 | `sync --check` is a read-only drift check; `sync --write` writes only changed files and refuses to overwrite a file without the generated marker unless forced | §3.14, §6 |
| 14 | Render is a pure function of model, bodies and settings: same input, byte-identical output | §6 |
| 15 | `check` and `verify` are read-only acceptance over the rendered result, including structural lint that ignores prose headings | §6, §3 (6) |
| 16 | ASCII UI catalog: generic type names (`panel`, `button`, ...) as defaults, `asciiui.types` overrides from S02, rendered ASCII spliced between markers; no parity check against project C# types | §3.7, §3.11 |
| 17 | Output mode is set per book and applies to every chapter of the book | §3.7 |
| 18 | Render reads a closed book's packed container directly, read-only and without extracting; an open book renders from its authoritative extracted state. Modifying commands keep the `open` requirement | §3.5 |


<a id="out-of-scope-10"></a>

### Out of scope

- Numbering values, number formats, anchors and reference resolution: S10 (the renderer calls into
  it; this scope does not decide anchor semantics).
- Authoring of footer, notes, status, badges, layout and index prose: S12.
- Library-wide sync across registered books and the README as the library book: S11.
- Container codec and atomic writes: S04.
- Grammar findings: S13.
- Model and command surface: S03, S07.


<a id="deliverables-9"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/render`: render pipeline, mode selection, heading emission, ToC, index, navigation,
  pruning, generated-file markers, output hashes.
- `internal/asciiui`: catalog, generic defaults, override resolution, block splicing.
- `internal/cli` command group for `sync` (`--check`, `--write`, `--prune`, `--force`) and `check` /
  `verify`.
- Golden-file fixtures: one small book rendered in all three modes; a book with notes, footer and
  index prose; a book with code fences and `####` prose.
- Tests: mode matrix, heading mapping matrix, prune matrix, drift detection, foreign-file protection,
  byte-identical re-render.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-9"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. Rendering the same fixture twice yields byte-identical files (hash comparison).
2. Monolith output contains the index followed by the full text; chapter-wise output writes one file
   per chapter plus the index README; part-wise output writes one file per part plus the index README.
3. Part-wise on a book without parts fails with a stable code; part-wise with two chapters sharing a
   part value produces one part file; duplicate part names are rejected.
4. The heading mapping matches the mode matrix exactly, including subchapters.
5. A `####` line in a body renders verbatim and appears in no ToC and no anchor table.
6. `sync --check` reports drift without writing; `sync --write` writes only changed files; a foreign
   file without the generated marker is not overwritten without `--force`.
7. Switching monolith -> chapter-wise -> monolith with `--prune` leaves exactly the generated files
   of the active mode.
8. Navigation in split files links the correct previous, index and next targets, omits the absent
   direction at a boundary, and places the footer above the bottom navigation; the README carries
   the Document Index link (library) or the Library and first-document links (other books).
9. `check` reports nothing for a clean fixture and reports a stable finding code for an injected
   structural defect; `verify` does not write.
10. `asciiui` renders identical output for the same spec with defaults, and applies an override from
    `asciiui.types`; no test references project C# types.
11. Index prose renders on its entry; an entry without prose renders unchanged.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-9"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- Generated file naming for chapters and parts: slug rules, transliteration, collision handling, and
  whether the number is part of the file name (`PLAN.md` forbids numbers in titles, not in names).
- The generated marker/banner format and its role in foreign-file protection.
- Where output hashes live (S04 hash pair) and what exactly is hashed.
- Index line format per mode, including the part grouping line and the depth limit (`index.depth`).
- ToC depth per mode and whether a `toc` setting can be `false`.
- Resolved (2026-11-05): navigation is visually identical to DocEngine. The labels are `← Previous`,
  `Index`, `Next →`, `← Library`, `First document →` and `Document Index`; split-file content is
  wrapped in `---` rules; the README carries top and bottom navigation derived from the library
  context and the footer sits above the bottom navigation. `toc` applies to split files; the
  monolith keeps the index.
- How the README title is derived (book metadata only; S03 stores it).
- Whether rendering a book into `Docs/<slug>/` is a store responsibility or a render responsibility;
  decide the seam with S11.
- ASCII UI spec syntax and marker syntax, and whether the catalog is data or code.
- What `check` reports versus what `verify` reports (overlap and difference).
- Resolved (2026-11-05): render reads a closed container read-only and never opens the book; the
  `open` requirement stays with modifying commands (`PLAN.md` §3.5). `check` and `verify` use the
  same read-only source.


<a id="risks-and-constraints-9"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- Output modes must not change the model. A mode is a render parameter, never a storage decision.
- Prose headings are text. Any code path that shifts, renumbers or indexes them violates `PLAN.md`
  §3 (6); the reference implementation does exactly that (`shift_headings`), so do not copy it.
- Determinism: map iteration, locale-dependent sorting and `time.Now()` are the usual leaks.
- The ASCII UI parity test from the reference implementation is explicitly not carried over.
- `sync --write` protecting foreign files is a safety property; test it with a hand-written file.


<a id="s10-numbering-anchors-and-references"></a>

## S10 — Numbering, Anchors and References ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05). Delivery slices: S10a (numbering, anchors, references, delivered).
Revision (2026-11-05, owner decision): IDs are immutable; the S10b rekey slice was removed. Placement
is a collection edit and duplicate ownership is a `sync --check` finding. The rekey text below is
historical. Cross-book reference resolution and link entries, deferred to S11, were delivered
retrospectively on 2026-11-05. The numbering hierarchy is fixed (chapters 1., subchapters 1.1).
Phase: 5. Depends on: S09 (render pipeline, heading emission). Blocks: S11, S12.
PLAN refs: §3 (8), §3.7 (numbering, anchors, references, reorder), §6 (references by stable ID,
anchors derived).


<a id="goal-10"></a>

### Goal

Make numbering an opt-in render-time property of the structure, keep anchors and references
independent of numbers and of titles, and provide ID-based cross-document references. IDs are
immutable: placement changes never rewrite a reference.


<a id="in-scope-10"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Numbering is opt-in; the library holds defaults and policy, the effective values are stored in the book manifest (storage by S07, policy by S11) | §3 (8), §3.7 |
| 2 | Numbers are added at render time when numbering is enabled; titles are stored without numbers | §3.7 |
| 3 | A numeric prefix in an incoming title (`1.`, `1.1`, `IV.`) is stripped during normalization, not rejected (normalization rule owned by S03) | §3.7 |
| 4 | Numbering applies to the structure tree; a `part` value creates no heading and does not affect numbering | §3 (10) |
| 5 | Anchors are number-independent: the heading anchor derives from the title or the ID, never from the number | §3.7 |
| 6 | Enabling, disabling or changing numbering never breaks a reference | §3.7 |
| 7 | Cross-document references target stable IDs of structure nodes and blocks; the visible anchor is derived at render time | §3.7, §6 |
| 8 | IDs are library-managed and unique across all books; global uniqueness is a deliberate constraint | §3.7 |
| 9 | Reordering regenerates numbering and all derived anchors and references in the same render | §3.7 |
| 10 | IDs are immutable: a move/reparent changes the ordered collections and leaves the ID and every reference valid; there is no rekey | §3.14 |
| 11 | Reference resolution: resolve an ID to its current location, detect dangling references, and report them as findings | §3.7, §6 |
| 12 | Deterministic anchor generation including Unicode titles, collision handling within a document and across documents | §3.7 |
| 13 | `link` entries participate in references; the link target is an ID, not a path | §3 (10) |


<a id="out-of-scope-11"></a>

### Out of scope

- Numbering and output-mode settings storage and command grammar: S07.
- Library defaults storage and policy: S11.
- Heading emission mechanics and output files: S09.
- ID creation, global uniqueness enforcement and the ID type: S03.
- Editorial regions and status: S12.
- Legacy Markdown links in the untouched legacy books: explicitly out of scope.


<a id="deliverables-10"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/refs`: ID reference type, resolution, rewriting, dangling detection, anchor derivation,
  collision handling.
- Numbering formatter integrated into the render pipeline (per-level format, optional per-book
  style), with the "titles are stored without numbers" guarantee.
- Reference resolution and rewriting helpers; no ID-changing operation.
- Tests: numbering toggle golden (headings change, anchors and references do not), reorder golden,
  duplicate-ownership finding, dangling reference finding, Unicode anchor fixtures, collision
  fixtures.
- This scope's implementation plan under `Planning/plans/`.


<a id="acceptance-criteria-10"></a>

### Acceptance criteria

1. With numbering off and on, the set of anchors and the resolved references is identical; only the
   visible numbers in headings differ (golden comparison).
2. Changing a numbering format (for example `1.` versus `1.1`) changes headings and leaves every
   anchor and reference valid.
3. Reordering two chapters renumbers them and updates all derived anchors and references in the same
   render; no reference dangles afterwards.
4. A move or reparent keeps the ID and every reference valid; duplicate ownership across books is a
   finding, not a rename.
5. A reference to a removed ID is reported as a finding with the referencing location.
6. Two chapters with the same title produce distinct anchors, deterministically and stably across
   renders.
7. A Unicode title produces a deterministic anchor and the same anchor on every platform.
8. Stored titles contain no numeric prefix after normalization; a title entered as `1.2 Ziel`
   renders as `1.2 Ziel` when numbering is enabled and as `Ziel` when it is disabled.
9. `part` values never appear in numbering and never emit a heading.


<a id="design-decisions-for-this-scope-s-planning-session-10"></a>

### Design decisions for this scope's planning session

- Per-level number format and whether it is configurable per book or fixed by the library policy.
- Anchor derivation: title slug, stable ID, or title slug with an ID suffix on collision. The choice
  determines link stability across renames; `PLAN.md` requires number independence and stable-ID
  references, not a specific anchor text.
- Slug algorithm: case folding, whitespace, punctuation and Unicode transliteration. Must be
  deterministic across platforms.
- Collision scope: per generated file, per book, or per library.
- Reference syntax in prose and in manifest links, and whether it may target a block or only a node.
- Whether dangling references are an error or a non-blocking finding, and in which command they
  surface (`check`, `verify`, render).
- Whether numbers can be part of generated file names (coordination with S09).


<a id="risks-and-constraints-10"></a>

### Risks and constraints

- Numbers creeping into anchors is the defect `PLAN.md` names. Test the toggle as a first-class
  acceptance criterion, not as an afterthought.
- IDs are immutable. Do not expose an ID-changing flag anywhere; a duplicate is reported by
  `sync --check`, never repaired by renaming.
- Legacy books are not read by the new tool. A reference to a legacy anchor is not a case the new
  system has to support.


<a id="s11-library-book-documentation-location-and-cut-over"></a>

## S11 — Library Book, Documentation Location and Cut-Over ![status: Final](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-Final-brightgreen?style=flat-square)

Status: implemented (2026-11-05); milestone close pending.
Revision (2026-11-05, owner decision): IDs are immutable and there is no rekey. Placement is a
collection edit; duplicate ownership is a `sync --check` finding. The rekey references in the
historical text below are superseded.
Phase: 6. Depends on: S02 (docs root), S04 (store, registry primitives), S05 (open state), S09
(render), S10 (references). Blocks: the dogfooding milestone.
PLAN refs: §3.1 (hard cut, library book as the exception), §3.6 (docs location), §3.8 (naming),
§3.9 (project boundary), §3 (1, 9), §3.7 (settings defaults, open books immovable), §6.


<a id="current-state-and-pre-planned-decisions-2026-11-05"></a>

### Current state and pre-planned decisions (2026-11-05)

Already implemented and to be used:

- `store.LoadRegistry` / `Registry.Save`: v1 `{version, books:[{id, path, kind}]}`. `path` is the
  output **directory** relative to the project. The library entry uses `.` (README at the project
  root); a regular book uses e.g. `Docs/guide`.
- `render.Service.Sync(book, outputDir, SyncOptions)`; `library sync` loops the registry and calls it
  per book with `--check`/`--write`/`--prune`/`--force`.
- `lifecycle.FromEnv`, `RequireClosed` and `State` for wiring and the open-book guard.
- IDs are immutable; there is no rekey. `move`/reparent change only the ordered collections, so
  references stay valid.
- `store.OpenBookCount` and the config mode guard already exist.
- `config.Values` exposes ProjectDir, StoreRoot, DocsRoot, UndoLimit and BookPointLimit.

Pre-planned decisions:

- `book new --id <id> --title <t>` creates the container from `model.NewManifest`, saves it closed,
  registers `{ID, Path: <docs-root-relative>/<slug>, Kind: "book"}`, and copies the library defaults
  into the manifest settings at creation (the model cannot express "unset").
- `library` command group: `library sync`, `book new`, `book move`, `book rename`,
  `book unregister`. Unregister deletes nothing; it removes only the registry entry.
- The library book is the registry entry with `Kind: "library"` and `Path: "."`; its monolith render
  is the repository `README.md`.
- Cut-over: create the library book from the current README content (structure plus blocks), render,
  and require `sync --check` clean. Do not touch legacy books.
- Open books cannot move, rename or unregister (`lifecycle.RequireClosed`).
- Render is the sole read path that bypasses the open state: it reads a closed book's container
  read-only, so the library-wide sync never opens a book. Body and structure mutations still require
  `open` (`PLAN.md` §3.5).
- IDs are issued by the library ledger and never change. A duplicate owned ID is corruption:
  `sync --check` rejects it with the ID and the affected books instead of renaming anything.


<a id="goal-11"></a>

### Goal

Make the library the structural authority over its books, create new books under the configured docs
root, and cut the CLABOK `README.md` over to a book generated by `pecia` — proving the model on a
real book while the legacy books stay untouched.


<a id="in-scope-11"></a>

### In scope

| # | Requirement | PLAN |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The library manages its books and maintains the repo `README.md` as its own monolithic book | §3 (1) |
| 2 | Library registry: entries for books (ID, kind, output path, state), the registry version, and the library's own entry | §3.2, §3.6 |
| 3 | Library-level defaults and policy for `numbering`, `toc`, `index.depth` and `output`, applied across books; per-book values stay in the book manifest | §3 (8), §3.7 |
| 4 | New books render into `Docs/` by default (docs root from S02); the library `README.md` stays fixed at the project root | §3.6, §3.11 |
| 5 | New-book authoring flow: create the book, choose the opt-ins, build the structure, then insert the prose | §3.1 |
| 6 | Hard cut: no migration, no import, no adopt; the new tool never reads legacy containers; the legacy tree is not changed, moved or deleted | §3.1, §3.9 |
| 7 | Library-wide sync: render every registered book and regenerate the library README index; report drift per book. Render reads a closed book's container read-only; modifying commands keep the open requirement. Cross-book `[[id:N]]` references and link entries resolve through the registry-wide layout map | §3 (1), §3.5, §3.7, §3.14 |
| 8 | Book move, rename and unregister update the registry and the output path; all three are refused while the book is open | §3.7 |
| 9 | The generated Document Index and the repository-layout block follow registry paths and the repository contents | §2.6, §3.14 |
| 10 | Product and CLI naming (`CLABOK`, `pecia`) is fixed; implementation file names may keep their names until a rename is planned | §3.8 |
| 11 | Cut-over: the current scaffold `README.md` becomes the first book, authored through the CLI, rendered at the project root, with `sync --check` clean | §3.1, §3.9 |
| 12 | The library book's structure, layout block, badges and index are the first real use of S09, S10 and S12 | §3.14 |

- Open/close state machine: S05.

<a id="deliverables-11"></a>

### Deliverables

- `internal/library`: registry model, defaults/policy, book discovery, library sync, move/rename/
  unregister guards.
- `internal/cli` command group `library` and `book new`.
- The first real book: its manifest, structure and bodies in the store, rendered to the project
  `README.md`.
- Cut-over runbook (short): what the scaffold README keeps, what moves into the book, how the clean
  `sync --check` is demonstrated.
